Started Bloodstained Ritual of the Night completely blindly. I have never played a metroidvania game before, but thoroughly enjoyed what Bloodstained had to offer. The game ain't without its shortcomings tho; in fact, there are quite few of them that hold back this latest entry in the franchise. Nonetheless, it has been a delightful experience.

Pros:
(+) Strong gameplay elements.
(+) Gazillions of weapons, items & skills for different types of play-styles (skills are absurdly fun).
(+) Obscene numbers of enemy variants & well-designed levels keep the experience always fresh & exciting.
(+) Big badass boss fighting.
(+) Grinding isn't a complete chore.
(+) Exploring the castle feels like an enthralling adventure.
(+) Atmosphere & soundtracks elevate the game.

Cons:
(-) Some of the worst (& lazy) side quests ever. Mostly fetch quests & killing 'x' numbers of enemies.
(-) Primary objectives aren't specified properly. Can get frustrating as you don't know what to do next.
(-) Balancing issues. Some skills that you get in earlier levels can carry you through the whole game, making it uninspiring to acquire (& level up) late-game skills.

Neutral:
(+/-) Okay-ish story. Not bad, not great either. Thankfully, everything else makes up for it.

N.B.- The story progression is linear. There are no choices in the game.

Brilliant game.

My time is low as on steam, as most of my play time is on PS4. I've been playing the PS4 version since the morning of Monday 17th. I'm finishing that version before I complete the game again on PC. I am an original backer and this game is everything I expected it to be. 

If you're a long term Castlevania fan, expect it to play like Dawn of Sorrow and a bit of OoE. It has all the expected tropes and cool Easter eggs hidden around the castle. The new weapons it has added also helps with varying the gameplay, along with many quests, masteries, and items to craft and complete. Once again, the fake ending appears like in all the other metroidvania games, so don't think you're finished if you defeat "the final boss". 

There is enough here to pay homage to the original Metroidvania games from years ago, while also adding enough for it to be worthy successor. I still enjoy using my familiars to find little hidden Easter eggs, or using them to find secret breakable walls to find items to upgrade my character. Little note, bring the Faerie familiar to the Piano in the Garden of Silence. 

Also, the game also adds in two difficulty modes, that increase enemy damage while also mixing up enemy placement. Adding a tonne of replay-ability to the game. Nightmare makes the game extremely difficult, and is fun if you want the challenge.

Finally, “13 Free DLCs” are on the way, and plenty of updates including a co-op mode. I will be coming back to this game for sure in the future, like I have with all the other Metroidvania games.

If you love Metroidvania then you should 100% be picking this up. 

EDIT : I did originally want this game to be pure 2D with sprites, however I've grown to like the 3D models use in game. They've also massively improved upon the graphics since when I played the original beta that was given to backers last year.

Verdict: 8/10 - I'm waiting for an sequel.

Bloodstained is a spiritual successor to Castlevania games, particularly the metroidvania ones, such as Symphony of the Night and Aria of Sorrow. It's clearly a product of passion of the lead developer behind those older Castlevania games but working outside of Konami. 

Anyone who's a fan of the Castlevania series would be at home here as a lot of the similar gameplay mechanics and vibes return here. In fact I'd go as far and say that they took the best aspects of all the Castlevania games and mixed them in here. The shard system is very reminiscent of Aria of Sorrow's soul system where we essentially can acquire enemy abilities by farming them. Here this system has been expanded into 5 types of shards, some acting as passive buffs, others as magical attacks of different types, and some being familiars that assist us. Some of the magic attacks are direction-based, allowing us to aim in any direction, which makes them even better and more fun to use and something we didn't have in Castlevanias.

The exploration and level design is just like we remember in those older Castlevania titles. A big castle full of different areas, each with its own theme, some of which can only be accessed after acquiring certain abilities or items. A few of the areas have been designed in very creative ways, such as the towers that are spiralling upwards in a circle and giving a pseudo-3D vibe. Save rooms, portal rooms, and boss rooms all make a return as does the familiar map design.

On top of the main questline, we can also do a few simple sidequests for NPCs, such as killing a certain monster type several times or bringing them a food item. All this helps with acquiring more items that can be used as crafting materials or ingredients for food. Crafting materials are used for making weapons, armour, trinkets and consumables, whereas food acts as a special type of consumable too in that it gives a stat bonus in addition to healing us (although I think the way food items work could've been explained a bit better!).

I really enjoyed the visuals and art style. Very colourful and detailed, and every area looked unique and breathtaking. Many of the areas are thematically similar to areas from Castlevania games - the castle entrance hallway, the garden, the library, the alchemy lab, the mechanical tower, the underwater caves, and so on. In each one we face their own unique challenges, both as enemy types and as traps of various kind. Boss fights were a bit of a mixed bag, some being too straight-forward, while others really fun and memorable. Some of the bosses were really creatively designed and the final fight was one of the best I've experienced in this type of game.

Music is stellar, which is no surprise, because the composer behind Castlevania soundtracks was involved in this game, so the style is very recognizable and you'll find yourself noticing and enjoying a track playing in virtually every area. Sound effects and voice acting are also brilliant.

Don't expect a superb story, but it's not bad either. The story is decent enough to keep you playing and exploring new areas and it doesn't seem to take up too much of your time. You're not forced into drawn out cutscenes and all the dialogues can be skipped with a press of a button, so no headache if you're replaying the game.

The game has a couple of bonus playable characters and some bonus modes to try too (which I'm yet to check out), so even after completing the main campaign, there's stuff to do and challenges to attempt. And the main campaign is longer than I remember it was in Castlevania games. Here it took me nearly 20 hours. Admittedly sometimes you might need to consult a walkthrough if you want to reach the game's true ending as some things will be a bit out there without any hints given. Just remember how obscure Symphony of the Night was in telling us about the inverted castle, and the same level of obscurity you'll have here. In fact almost too much like that if we take into account the boss fight that gives us the first fake ending.

I've greatly enjoyed every moment of playing Bloodstained. Sure, there are a few minor criticisms here and there, particularly relating to too much backtracking in places and a few obscure moments of being stuck, but generally, this was amazing and nostalgic. This game was made for people who loved Castlevania games and, as far as quality and fun, it can safely stand side-by-side with giants such as Symphony of the Night and Aria of Sorrow.

[strike]Castlevania: Symphony of the Night[/strike] Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night is a phenomenal game, and the 22,427 other reviews at the time of this writing agree with me. I'm not saying anything controversial, groundbreaking or surprising when I tell you that [strike]Castlevania: Portrait of Ruin[/strike] Bloodstained is a game you should be playing already.

[strike]Castlevania: Order of Ecclesia[/strike] Bloodstain's main character, [strike]Shanoa[/strike] Miriam is not a vampire and uses kickass powers taken from the enemies you encounter over the course of the game. [strike]Alucard[/strike] Miriam is a character defined first and foremost by being a super awesome unstoppable badass and the list of weapons that [strike]Soma Cruz[/strike] Miriam has available, along with the incredible amount of powerups and skills she can collect, boggles the mind.

Castlevania is dead. Long live [strike]Castlevania[/strike] Bloodstained.

Also in the years since release there's been a ton more added to this game and I can confirm everything feels pretty awesome and I highly recommend giving all the bonus stuff a go after your first playthrough.

If you hate this game, that's OK, but I think that's really something you should be talking with your therapist about because whatever horrible damage you've suffered in life is something you need to work through and get past so the healing can begin.

You like Castlevania: Symphony of the Night? You can buy this with closed eyes, you'll be right at home. You never touched SotN? Go play it. It is a timeless classic in which most of what is known as the "Metroidvania" genre takes its roots (the "-vania" part at least).

For those who don't know what I'm writing about, Metroidvanias are 2D platformers with RPG elements and a big emphasis on exploration, a formula nailed down more than 20 years ago by Koji Igarashi (IGA for the initiated), the very same guy behind Bloodstained: RotN.

Saying this would seem anecdotal at first glance but I couldn't put enough emphasis on how much Bloodstained borrows from its spiritual grand-forefather, nearly to a fault as it feels sometimes like a time capsule of a long gone era, one that forgot to take risks and evolve the traditional formula. But it displays such a mastery and dedication to the core tenants of the genre that it is hard to hold it against its creator.

In terms of game design, RotN is solid. Myriam - the female protagonist - plays well, the controls are reactive and your character, initially quite slow, will get much faster as you unlock new movement options. 

IGA also polished many of the side features of the previous Castlevania titles. For instance, in most games, cooking would be treated just as an alternate way to heal your character. In this case, the many dishes also grant permanent stat boosts. A very good reason to explore every nooks and cranies in search of rare ingredients. You also have many options to build your own version of Myriam, with numerous comsetic options and different end-games weapons in the same power range, as opposed to the ubiquitous Alucard sword found in its venerable ancestor. 

Speaking of replayability, the game is already 15 to 20 hours long on the first playthrough but also offers multiple difficulties for those who'd like to revisit it with an additional challenge. And then there are multiple characters to play (including some bosses), alternate game modes and even an item randomizer to spice up things on each new playthrough.

My only reservation would the artistic direction, with its competent but uneven 3D graphics and animations, garish colors and lacking a global sense of homogeneity. This is luckily not too much of a deterrent and shouldn't prevent most - except maybe the most picky aesthetes out there - to enjoy their time with this gothic-anime extravaganza.

So yeah, at the risk of repeating myself: if you're longing for a revival of the 2D exploration-based Castlevania of yore - or wish to discover where it all began - this title is a must-have.

Metroidvanias aren't terribly plentiful, though they're not the rarest genre of game. I suppose perhaps that "good" Metroidvanias are few and far between, though. I don't claim to be an expert on them, or their biggest fan, but there is a certain charm to exploring an area, finding spots you can't get into, then waiting until you have an ability or item that lets you obtain more goodies and explore further. This bleeds over a bit into other games/genres, such as keys and puzzle pieces in Resident Evil games to push further into unexplored regions of the mansion, police station, etc., and even immersive sims like Deus Ex Human Revolution (punch through walls or get a high jump) and Prey 2017 (turn into a coffee mug and roll into areas you can't otherwise enter, etc.). It's pretty fantastic and even if Metroidvanias aren't my favorite genre, I cannot deny their appeal, and I am quite eager to find more that I enjoy.

Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night was certainly a largely enjoyable game for me. The graphics are some of the best I think I've seen in a mostly-2D Metroidvania (though Dust: An Elysian Tale's *art style* appeals to me more), the voice acting is pretty darn good (David Hayter (Solid Snake) voices one of the main characters), the game controls pretty well, the sound effects and music are good, and...yeah, it's a rather solidly made game.

The only complaints I really have are that I tend to enjoy Metroidvanias that are a bit more "compact." This one went on for so long that I got a little bored at one point...and it actually made me want to play Super Metroid again...so I did! I played through that for the second time in my life a couple of days ago, and finished it in just under 8 hours (I turned the whole map pink and tried to find all the stuff with as little walkthrough-searching as possible). It's not perfect, but the brevity and atmosphere of that game are pretty dang great. Anywho, back to Bloodstained. I spent over 35 hours completing this game, an I wasn't even achievement-hunting, or trying to 100% everything. I just tried to kill all the bosses, explore all the areas, etc., and it still took a long time for a Metroidvania, at least in my opinion.

Oddly enough, I found the game's difficulty to be horribly balanced. Early on, I was getting my butt handed to me and I was exclaiming profanities during an early boss fight as there just wasn't much I could do to beat the guy except for raw skill. I had the best weapon I could get my hands on that I was aware of at the time, I had killed a bunch of monsters (I killed over 6,400 by the end of the game) to level up a few times for better damage and defense, I had the best defensive gear I could get equipped, and I was still having a really rough time beating the second boss. As time went on, though, my skill level wasn't getting *that* much better, but once food recipes are available in high supply (they give you permanent stat boosts on the first consumption per foodstuff), I was curb-stomping bosses left and right.

In fact, bosses became incredibly easy the further I went into the game. When I killed the final boss, I literally stared in confusion and asked "Was that really the end?" and soon enough, the credits rolled. I am not exaggerating when I say that the final boss was probably the easiest boss fight in the game, even though it's supposed to be the most powerful thing in the entire game. Now I will say that I'm not a big challenge-seeker, or a Dark Souls fan or anything of the sort. I'm fine with easy games. I just like games to be well-balanced, so if the whole thing is easy, fine, and if the whole thing is challenging, then that makes sense, too. Where things are weird for me is when an early boss wipes the floor with me, but the later bosses are a joke. Opening up more gear to craft and meals to prepare before the second boss would have made for a smoother difficulty curve for people who aren't very talented such as myself, while the hardcore folks could just refrain from the meals for a challenge, and so forth.

So really, aside from the game taking longer than I like a Metroidvania to take, and the difficulty curve feeling very wrong/weird, I didn't have too many gripes about this game, which is really saying something because complaining is a special skill of mine, for better or for worse. The story was better than most Metroidvanias, though nothing amazing. The characters weren't phenomenal, but they were alright. The game was longer than I like the genre to be, but it wasn't so long that I didn't ever want to bother finishing it. Oh, and while options are nice and everything, I found there to be too many Shards (equippable magical relics which give you special attacks/spells), as a bunch of them were crap, and having so much trash clogging up space in my inventory was a bit of an annoyance. Just a set number of really good abilities like in games such as Super Metroid would have been preferable for me, and I say that as someone who isn't into nostalgia.

Anyway, it's not an amazing game, but I thought it was pretty darn good, and don't regret dropping $19.99 on it while it was on sale. =)

[h1]Bloodstained is a masterpiece for a lost generation[/h1]

Starting out with Symphony of the Night, and working through the entirety of the 90's, up to 2011 on every single castlevania game made in that era, Koji Igarashi is quite literally "daddy castlevania"

That said, this is his latest work, and quite frankly a crowning jewel on two decades of some of the best games in the genre, that both sparked an entire new genre and franchise which proved lucrative to both Konami* and Koji himself.

Following corporate shenanigans, Koji was told there was no more room in this world to create yet another gothic action adventure game, and told him to busy himself with other things. Koji said no. Koji left. Koji was handed ~6m US by his loyal fanbase and Koji spent the last 6 years building this masterpiece.

[h1]Actual review[/h1]

--<> Story <>--

Bloodstained: Ritual of the night is, as mentioned before, a masterpiece in it's genre. There will be heavy referencing to other works he made so if you haven't yet, be sure to play those as well.

It follows the story of Miriam, a girl recently awoken from a decade long slumber, Jonathan, a member of the alchemist guild and close friend of Miriam and Gebel, one of Miriam's old friends with a troubled past.

Along the way, many other characters of interest are introduced in beautifully executed cutscenes which are very reminiscent of Symphony of the night, which is worth points all of it's own.

There's a good story buildup, Strong interactions whenever they take place, clear dialogue, humorous tidbits, drama, excitement, despair. The writing is on point and to the letter, creating an engaging plotline that satisfies to the very end.


--<> Gameplay <>--

This is a treat to exposition on, and one of the reasons this genre of game does so very very well, regardless of what the corporate machine might say.

It's a 2.5D game this time, sharing both old and new mechanics that span two decades worth of creative engineering with the games in question. The soul system from Aria / dawn of sorrow sees it's return as the shard system, but fleshed out, more versatile and way more engaging than it's predecessors.

Aria / Dawn featured an Active, Passive, Channeled (sustained) and utility type. Bloodstained features all of that, a new directional active alternate and Familiar type.

Lets start with the directional active. It's a fully 360 degree aimable active ability that can also be used unaimed as a quick flick. This alone adds so much more possibilities to your arsenal, it's worth giving it its own little mention. Many of the progression abilities in this game hinge on this, but it neither feels gimmicky or uselessly added. Again, bonus points here.

The rest of the gameplay is as you'd expect if you're familiar with the series. You start off as an aspiring young maiden with a pair of boots and some personal effects, yet you end as a demigod, literally flying through areas, laying waste to anything that dares oppose you.

It has the item system seen in Portrait of Ruin most comparatively, the quest design from Order of Ecclesia and the overall layout of Harmony of Dissonance / Symphony of the night. Everything feels natural despite the transition to 2.5D, every living thing in it's environment breathes atmospheric righteousness and it's clear to see what two decades of experience amounts to.

The RPG system makes a return, as has been staple since Symphony, The clock tower, library and other such classic areas have returned as well, and overall it's done exactly the way it should have been. If you are already a fan of the series, you will absolutely devour this and enjoy every second of it.


--<> Music & Sound <>--

Being labeled famous for its grandiose musical scores, upbeat strings and memorable tunes, it should come as no surprise that this once again delivers as one would have expected, given they have resorted to the original franchise's composers yet again.

I could go on about how good this is, but take this as an example, and apply it to the rest:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fRAQ-ZzOE4M

It is by any standard exactly as it should be, yet does not try to copy its older iterations, creating and composing an entirely new original score that is heavily influenced by it's predecessors, yet still manages to create and introduce an entirely original and excessively satisfying audial experience.

The game's sound effects are well decided upon, well crafted, feel right at home in their environment and bring everything together.

So, F*ck yes, bonus points.


--<> Final Verdict <>--

You may have seen this at the first line of the review, but I'm not joking or exaggerating. This is a masterpiece in it's genre. It's a game born out of love and dedication towards two decades of creative worldbuilding, a story spanning many years and culminating in getting stopped by an entity that has no business deciding that for the rest of us.

It's the piece of art labeled as "Spite" yet portraying the most wonderfully shaped form you could imagine.

It's everything your mom warned you about when you were little, yet in a gentlemanly form that has no malicious intent.

It's everything that's right in the world in the face of adversity and hatred.

It's Bloodstained: Ritual of the night.

It's the most Castlevania game in it's franchise, and it was created for us by a man whose dedication knows no bounds.

Thank you Iga. Thank you so much.

I don't know what to say about this one. Is it the best Metroidvania ever made? Is it worth whatever price you find it at? Am I eagerly awaiting The Scarlet Engagement?

The answer to all these questions is "Yes."

Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night carries on the legacy of the Castlevania games, and is clearly the culmination of many years of experience and expertise. The mastermind behind it knows what makes the genre work, and blends it all together in a package here that has more content than anyone knows what to do with. While my hours played is well over 200 (and those are real hours played, not a result of simply leaving the game open by mistake), it's because I speedrun the game, not because I've seen everything it has to offer. I've still barely touched Classic Mode or Classic Mode 2 (admittedly, the latter of which is DLC). 

There are four characters with whom you can go through the normal game, each with their own unique abilities, similar to how previous Castlevania games would have an Albus Mode or Julius Mode. While these are a bit bare compared to Miriam Mode (the default/main character), each still provides the amount of content you'd get from any Metroidvania you'd pick up here on Steam. 

It certainly isn't a coincidence that the subtitle for this game is only one word off from "Symphony of the Night." This game takes everything SOTN did, does it better, and then multiplies it by ten. There's a huge variety of weapons to choose from, though you'll probably make the mistake of sticking with the basic swords for your first run, as I did, neglecting some of the more amazing weapons, like the Scythe, or the simple Kung Fu Shoes, whose technique Flashing Air Kick allows some truly glorious sequence breaking. If Melee isn't your thing, that isn't a problem either, as every enemy in the game (except one, the basic Morté, what would be called a Zombie in Castlevania) has a Shard to drop, and every Shard allows Miriam to access a new ability, be it a fire spell, a summoned chainsaw, a familiar, or the ability to turn the entire world upside down--like the upside-down castle of Symphony of the Night, except you control it and can switch it on and off any time you want. 

Truly a masterpiece. 

Ritual of the Night nails the experience of starting the player weak and without much to do ability-wise, and then slowly progressing and powering up the player until you are a goddess rampaging through the castle and destroying everything in sight. Unusually, though, Miriam is not truly weak and powerless from the start, if you know how to use the abilities she begins the game with. While you may frown upon seeing the basic and seemingly-weak Kung Fu Shoes as the starting weapon, you should be aware that the Kung Fu Shoes are a primary staple of speedruns, and are far from useless, even if you aren't trying to reach places you shouldn't be able to reach yet. 

You might think, with so many shards to be collected, that it's a grindfest, but this problem is expertly dodged by two facts. First is that every shard has a 4% base droprate, minus one or two outliers. This means that, at worst, an enemy may need to be killed 25 times before you get their shard, which is a huge improvement over some of the 0.5% droprates that some Metroidvanias have. However, the second stroke of genius is that Luck is your most useful stat, and there are ways to begin boosting it very early on. Luck has a direct and noticeable effect on drop rates for items and shards, and is the single most important stat to stack through the game. If you're anything like me, you'll reach an area full of new enemies and immediately feel the need to grind it out until you have the shard from every enemy. Unlike many games, though, it doesn't feel like a drag here, as you'll spend a few minutes doing that, and then you'll be ready to move on. You'll never spend 20 minutes grinding against a single enemy to get their shard, something I've done far too many times in Aria of Sorrow and Dawn of Sorrow. 

It simply feels good to do this. While there are many shards of questionable utility (like Summon Toad), just as many are surprisingly useful, and the desire to know whether an enemy gives something good or something useless is easily enough to compel players to grind them all out. And, importantly, it never really feels like grinding, except on those rare movements that you find the Augment Luck shard and realize that it's in your best long-term interests to stop everything and grind out 9 of them to max out its potential. That can actually take a while, but usually it's Rank you'll want to increase, which is done somewhere else, and not Grade, which is increased by collecting duplicates of the shard. 

That "other place," where you increase Rank, is with Johannes, who provides access to the crafting system, the cooking system, and the shard upgrade system. This is the only area where I've found any flaws in the game, as it's all a bit obtuse and unclear. It's mostly a UI problem, because some weapons require other weapons in order to be crafted, making some armor and weapon crafting like a tree, while everything is presented as a list. It isn't too much of an issue, but it is an issue, made worse by the fact that you'll also need to find recipes in the castle to make certain things. 

Good luck trying to figure out why you can't craft a Tea Dress because it doesn't even show up on your list, making you think you need a recipe, when really it's just that you don't have any Durable Rags and you used the last Cotton you had making Bat Wings... Since you don't have any of the materials required, it simply won't show up on your list of craftable items. Like I said, it can be obtuse. 

Graphically, the game is beautiful, and musically it has all the awesomeness you'd expect of a Castlevania game--because this is, in everything but name, the ultimate Castlevania. 

I've played a lot of Metroidvanias. Gal Guardians, Ender Lilies, AfterImage, Blasphemous, Hollow Knight, Castlevania: Dominus Collection, I could go on. But there's no need. We can add a hundred more to that list, and the result would be the same--Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night is the best of them. It's no contest. If you like Metroidvanias, then you need to play this. It's the best.

Bloodstained could perhaps best be described as a love letter to Castlevania: SOTN. There is so much fan service in this game that any fan of the original Metroidvania would notice and appreciate the call backs. The backstep, the enemy design, the castle secrets, the fast travel system, and the unlocking of new abilities all feel enjoyable to use. Interestingly, the more I played, the more I felt that this game actually does SOTN better than SOTN did. 

What I liked about this game: 

- Exploring the castle is enjoyable and it doesn't feel too linear, although the game's path is not as open as something like Hollow Knight. For those cartographers that enjoy exploring every inch of the castle, this game definitely fulfills that desire in spades. 

- There are a huge amount of power-ups and abilities to unlock, and most of them are good enough that it comes down to player preference than choosing the best ability. There are some abilities and weapons that stand out over others, of course, but you never feel like you are locked down into a particular play style. 

- For reference I played on normal. ROTN has a solid difficulty curve. It starts you off with difficulty appropriate bosses and builds you up over time. I never felt like I needed to grind on anything to get strong enough to beat a boss rather than simply learning their moves and getting better at the fight. Some of the later bosses can be quite difficult, but there are always options for those that feel they are stuck. Since food healing items in this game are quite unlimited, players can make a boss as difficult as they want it to be, although I think the best way to play is to limit how many healing items you want for an appropriate challenge. 

- The late game power boost is much appreciated. I like it when a game isn't afraid to give you really cool abilities once you've reached the end. It is really fun to have gone from struggling to survive to becoming the boss that enemies fear. 

- The crafting system is pretty cool. I enjoyed the cooking system and the permanent stat buffs it gives. Also, the game would keep a log of item drops so you'd always know where to go to get what you need. I think the cooking in this game is one of the better ways to do food buffs. 

Things I didn't like: 

- The dual grinding system for shards felt like a bit much. ROTN in this respect definitely doesn't respect player's time with frequent items/shard drops rates of 2% or less. Having to grind out both the grade and the rank of abilities felt really annoying. I think the game would have been better if they only had ranks or grades for shards and were more liberal with drop rates. It's a single player game and running in and out of a room to kill the same guy over and over for a 2% drop isn't particularly engaging or fun. 

- Some of the late game content has very little guidance. I did unfortunately have to look up a guide at one point because I didn't understand how to progress to the next area, and I found myself thinking, I probably would have not have figured this out on my own (example: the water area). I think adding some hints or something from the NPCs would probably have made my experience a little better, but this only happened in the late game, and for the most part progression was fine. 

Overall: 10/10. The negatives were only minor points in an otherwise wonderful game. I'd recommend it. It is one of the few games on Steam that I 100%'d.

Bloodstained Ritual of the Night (RotN) is an interesting game. I’ll start with the positives and then head into my criticisms. 

First of all I want to say the transition from 2D to 3D had me worried about how the game would feel, I was delightfully surprised that movement, mechanics, and combat felt just like Symphony of the Night (SotN) or at least very close. It's not like the transition from 2D to 3D for other games have all been bad but they tend to feel heavier and clunkier than their 2D counterparts historically. This, however, was not the case.

Other positives, music is pretty decent, lots of synthesizer and felt very playstation-era in some compositions. Animations were fluid and well defined for every character.  The dialog and voice acting is decent. I wouldn’t stay it’s the best, quite frankly I only mention it because I’m glad to see David Hayter get work who was by far the best voice actor in the game. I wish to see him do more voice acting in our post-MGS world.

On to criticisms, RotN suffers from a lot of impostor syndrome and unfortunately that really leads to a gray area of being an excellent follow up to SotN to being almost a subpar clone that doesn't have the same magic as the original. Most of the time, especially late game, the latter is more true than the former. Mind you this game can exist in its own space without referencing SotN at all, but it's a bit hard, considering if you played the source material the amount of parallelism is very apparent (even down to the name of the game) and it is difficult to not back reference it and look at it in comparison.

This game also has an issue of rewarding you for your time. There were secrets that we (my brother and I played this together) found by accident but the reward for them was nothing (or worse than nothing, worthless). Rooms with keys that don’t give you anything cool, special cutscenes that spawn a monster (if you played this game you know what I’m talking about) that gives you a shard that’s mostly worthless (if you’re lucky), etc. This is a common issue.

Another issue that was extremely frustrating, there is a part of the game that is completely dependent on your progression of the map purely by luck. [spoiler] You need a shard to ‘swim’ and there is one enemy you need to kill to get it and it doesn’t drop first try. [/spoiler] That’s insane and a massive waste of time because there is no real hint for that and you spent the last two hours trekking the castle to find what you thought you missed. (Mind you SotN had the clock room, but at least there is a hint for it)

Furthermore, the game is riddled with shard overload, 90% of the shards in the game are useless I hate to say. Really there are a few core shards and you stick with them. There is even one shard you get at the end of the game that is sick, but you use it once and that is it. It almost seems like a worthless mechanic when you compare it to castlevania subweapons which actually have a tactical advantage in fights both normal and bosses paired with the abilities you learn in SotN.

End of the day, if you’re into metroidvania and/or you like the SotN you should play this game. It is fun, and it’s a good time, and worth your money. Its run length for a full castle / good ending is anywhere in the 10-15 hour range depending on how clever you are on a first playthrough. However, don’t expect it to exceed the masterpiece that SotN is. I certainly didn’t go into it thinking it would, but as I said earlier, it's hard not to hold it against it.

[h1]What is Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night?[/h1]
Bloodstained is the archetypal Metroidvania game, featuring elements so strikingly similar to the very same Castlevania games that helped spawn the subgenre, that you would be forgiven for thinking it was part of Konami's beloved series. In truth, Bloodstained was crowdfunded under the watchful eye of Koji Igarashi, the very same man who is often credited with helping cement the genre through his work on many Castlevania games, including Symphony of the Night and Aria of Sorrow. Bloodstained is no more than a spiritual successor to these titles, but their influence is felt throughout the entire game, with numerous notable parallels even beyond the basic mechanics.


[h1]Basic Information[/h1]
Within the main scenario of Bloodstained, the player controls Miriam: a shardbinder who has been in some sort of magical slumber for the past decade, only just now waking with the appearance of a mysterious, demon-infested castle. After some light cutscenes and exposition setting this premise up, the player is set free to explore the surrounding ship and eventual castle, limited only by their ability to defeat foes and collect shards or items that will enhance Miriam, enabling greater freedom of exploration.

Defeating demons has a chance to grant Miriam the power of a shard. Shards exist within a handful of different types, including passive types that enhance Miriam's power, or active abilities such as double-jumping or firing energy blasts. Collecting multiple copies of these shards and separately enhancing them through alchemy will grant further power to these abilities. Along with weapons, armor, and accessories, the player can customize various loadouts to take advantage of their collection, and allow them to swap on the fly.


[h1]The Good[/h1]
+ The core gameplay of exploration and combat is very solid, being incredibly similar to the aforementioned Symphony of the Night and Aria of Sorrow. I found trying to master the movement mechanics to be especially entertaining early on

+ Alchemy is a fun diversion that allows for the creation and enhancement of Miriam and her equipment, all while being optional. You can even change up Miriam's look very slightly to give her a more personal touch

+ A variety of additional modes are unlocked at the start of the game, and it seems more are being added with further updates

+ The voice acting was surprisingly good if you don't mind the campy script. I also particularly enjoyed the music, and the overall presentation is pretty solid


[h1]The Bad[/h1]
- It is incredibly easy to make Miriam overpowered only a little ways into the game. Bloodstained also allows for similar healing to Breath of the Wild (inventory full of healing you collected for use at any time), so you will have to impose restrictions on yourself to maintain a challenge

- Many of the most entertaining and/or useful shards occupy the same slot and generally serve the same purpose. There are also multiple shards required for progression which must be swapped for throughout the game that will slow the pace to a crawl momentarily, and it quickly becomes a nuisance

- There are hints for progression that are given one-time-only by vendor NPC's that you may find yourself skipping repetitive dialogue for, causing you to accidentally miss vital information. Even with these hints, there are still a couple points of progression that are straight up obtuse, and you might just get lost and have to consult a guide


[h1]Your Mileage May Vary[/h1]
~ Bloodstained often feels like a carbon copy of other Castlevania titles, blurring the line between homage and repeat. Maybe you don't mind an extremely familiar experience, or maybe you expect more innovation

~ If you are experienced in the genre, Hard mode is likely where you will want to start the experience, but you must input a code or otherwise beat the game on Normal first. Hard is still arguably too easy, and Nightmare mostly frontloads the difficulty

~ The story is fairly blasé and unremarkable, in my opinion


[h1]The Verdict[/h1]
If you like Metroidvanias, especially the -vania part of the genre, then this game is a no-brainer. You will feel right at home with the setting and mechanics, and there is genuine fun to be had in exploring and slaying demons. If you enjoy a challenge, simply be mindful of the lengths you will go to farm/grind the things you want. This is not ideal, but I estimate the game to have a 15-20 hour runtime on a blind playthrough, depending on how lost you get. This makes starting a new playthrough a fairly easy ask, and you can even play with the extra modes if you desire a change of pace. $40 is a bit high of a price if you only plan to play through the game once, in which case I would recommend waiting for a sale.

Anyone who has played a Metroidvania style game knows exactly what they should feel like, and Bloodstained absolutely nails it.

Everyone keeps drawing Symphony comparisons and rightfully so, but know before you dive in: this game plays more like Aria of Sorrow/Dawn of Sorrow, with the Enemy Skills you obtain through Shards being a major component of gameplay. 

Cannot recommend this enough if you've enjoyed a Castlevania game in the past 20 years.

[h1]THE GOODS[/h1]

weapons are varied

same feel you've come to expect from older iga titles, but works off of the charisma that order of ecclesia had going for it

absolutely huge castle with tons to explore

the controls, while in places stiffer than in other metroidvanias, have a logic to them that isn't bad which expects your mastery

this isn't like SOTN where you can facetank half the bosses to death because they just happened to make cool designs and didn't really think about how alucard would interact with them, this is working off of boss design principles refined throughout the DSvania trilogy

crafting system really doesn't get in the way and rewards you for existing generally; you still find a lot of goodies in the walls like any good metroidvania game

also, generally, after you've crafted something like a food item once, you can just like, buy more

most money comes from chests around the castle in bursts, but you can also make it from selling shards you're never going to use, or ambiently collecting tiny amounts from light sources (this means that if you're not wise with your resources, you have to do without)

exploration is a really strong point, and revisiting areas of a castle for the serial nature of experiencing the areas again has never been quite so strong

i'm a big fan of zangetsu because of doing solo runs as him in curse of the moon, so i'm hype for zangetsu mode

i can see really enjoying this on the higher difficulties, especially after playing normal, particularly for the serial nature of some of the areas; nightmare seems hard enough to justify NG+ing onto it even, but mileage may vary

variety of elemental environments and length to the equip system really makes me want to play again on a higher difficulty just so i can get some actual mileage out of everything (particularly nightmare because that might be just want i wanted out of a metroidvania)

[h1]THE neutral[/h1]

the bosses can get teeth-grittingly difficult if you don't decide to really specialize your moveset, and even then...!

some things in the game either expect you to get lost more or don't know their place (looking at you, quest and crafting requirements)

to elaborate on what i mean by that, sometimes the crafting materials for things aren't things you'd have on hand, so if you really want something for a damage type build or armor, you might have to do some specific hunting, not that that's unfun or anything, i'm just incredibly impatient with my games these days so i don't do that

also, the common crafting materials are in the respawning blue chests in various areas, so if you end up doing any backtracking (and it's a metroidvania game so you're gonna do some) you can pick 'em up almost instinctually as you see a chest and go "ooo chest" and proceed to inhale its contents

some bugs, game might seem like it lacks polish at times

[h1]THE BAD[/h1]

- sometimes the boss design doesn't feel fair, even on normal; some things just feel like you have no intelligent way of dodging without using cheesy shards that let you tank

it feels kind of a step down from the sorrow series, OoE and portrait of ruin, where a lot of fights you could very conceivably do for ten minutes with level 1 crook loot and still win because you could avoid being hit

provided, in every metroidvania/igavania, you can just get pinged by the mooks because they were always a little more erratic than the bosses

here, the 3D models of the enemies make hitboxes a nightmare to reason with, and you're gonna want to use polearms if you don't want to take a lot of clumsy contact damage

- tries too hard to follow some of the same beats of sotn, which is somewhat the point for nostalgia's sake, but in doing this it copies some of sotn's esoteria behind its puzzles too; not the worst thing ever honestly but yeah

- doesn't [i]quite[/i] give the same thematic punch as dracula and movie monsters, and in that sense i wish the game crossed over into eastern mythology more to capitalize on a different kind of, shall we say, thematic reverence

at the same time, it did a really good job establishing its own uniqueness and retaining european roots with a little cool japanese stuff mixed in

- if you like the classicvanias for their unique feels, you might dislike even the suggestion of grinding here; you can beat it on normal pretty much without grinding, bu~t you might feel the want to grind for cool items in some places, and it's always available

overall the pacing on levelling up and gear might put you off from experiencing areas again; after all, the challenge in them has passed and you don't wanna kinda just mill about in them

...if you play on NIGHTMARE, you're capped at level 1, so that's not so much a problem. enter NIGHTMARE in all caps in file select to uncap the difficulty if you're certain you're an epic pro gamer (you can rename it later too!)

- the boss thematic design is a step down from Curse of the Moon, where even the midst bosses were painted as grandiose, here they're just kind of... here. like, the heck happened to electric peacock man? why's he just essentially shard fodder in some unremarkable room? i get SoTN had some moments like this, but dang...

- stop making me SWITCH TO THE REFLECTOR RAY FREAKIN'

- or, rather, i always hate when metroidvanias make you seriously dig through your inventory, it's annoying

- boss HP should be a skill shard instead of an equip tbh (not that they're a metroidvania staple, but they help the pace of fights a lot i feel, particularly in this game specifically)

[h1]addressing common criticisms others have of the game[/h1]

[b]voice acting and horror game-related opinions[/b]

if there's any campyness left in the voice acting, i'm gonna attribute that to wanting to retain some cheesy qualities (which after all sotn got by on); they definitely wanted to build their own charisma and character with this game, and some of that goes against what people consider objective quality for a game

myself, i never notice things like voice acting, but i actually feel like a lot of the main voice acting of this game is at least refined, and while some bosses can be cheesy, like... that's the point, igavania titles have never been hard silent hill horror, they've been an exploration of fear elements in game design, meanwhile the theme has typically been vaguely cheesy

this hearkens back to the NES era where simon had it hardest; the delay on his whip was to instate solid, clear rules to the player (who is otherwise mistaken that the controls aren't quite thought out) and also put tension into fighting monsters

hits had to count, you had to know how to position yourself, etc.

of course, this doesn't always lend itself well in the NES eras, but this shows the strongest in the PC Engine [i]Rondo of Blood[/i]

the bosses aren't out to scare you by being dark or gorey (although some are gorey!), they're out to scare you by being what they are and then kicking the shehehe out of you

so, in essence, the game tries harder to be "cool nineties video game" with hints of the OoE personality than it does silent hill

[b] graphics [/b]

well-optimized, very pretty, and honestly, i love 'em

while nothing can run at native res (1920x1080) on my level 5 archcrook computer, one size down suits this game just fine

as always, you can whack vsync and some shadows and effects and the game will run just fine most of the time

detail in areas varies, which can also effect low-tier PC performance, but in boss encounters and high combat they generally know when to leave it alone and let you try not to die

i don't really get what people still complaining about the visuals are expecting at this point, i feel like, even if one is unimpressed, it's both a 2D-centric title, and it's not really supposed to be a blockbuster in terms of graphics, it's supposed to be a good game

I have played many Metroidvanias in my life, I have finally given Bloodstained the investment it deserves and from my experience, this review will explain to you why this game is worthy of your game library.

Bloodstained is a series done by Koji Igarashi, the main director for the majority of Castlevania games until his eventual leave from Konami, Bloodstained is in essence a spiritual successor to the Castlevania games that came before.

Let's go over the gameplay, something I found to be great is how the combat weapons as well as shards give so many options to playstyle and player expression, you can fight with big swords, pistols, whips, katanas, normal swords and many more, each possessing a secret special input like in Street Fighter, which can be either accidentally discovered or be found throughout the castle through books.

Shards, which is the main gimmick of this game function in essence similarly to how souls or glyphs worked in Castlevania Aria of Sorrow and Castlevania Order of Ecclesia respectively, the difference here is that shards can be strengthened through either obtaining copies or strengthening it through enhancements through NPCs, this encourages grinding and experimentation with what you prefer.

The exploration and map design was also superb to me as finding secrets was extremely fun, with each map having amazing music from the Castlevania composer Michiru Yamane. For example the map is so huge that there are dev rooms, secret bosses, and at least 5 additional areas if you want to aim for the true ending of the game.

Speaking of which, I found the story to once again be great from Igarashi's side of things, the mystery of Shardbinders, the dynamic between Miriam and Gebel, Zangetsu and etc. The ending had a bittersweet ending which left things in the air for a potential sequel.

Something I think is very important for a metroidvania is, "are the bosses good" and from my experience it's some of the best in the series. Take for example Bloodless, the patterns were extremely well designed where a bad player would not die from being underleveled or having bad gear, but rather by not paying attention to the environment. For example one attack she does which can instantly kill is when she performs a "Blood rain" attack and you must stand under the umbrellas to not get hit. There are many more bosses which hold more spectacle but those would be my examples.

Other things I liked which I complained about Hollow knight is that the map here actually makes sense, since it's on a grid system and appears for you on the top right screen. Another thing I preferred is that the combat here gives a lot more variation and a means of expression, that is also seen in the traversal as traversing through enemies becomes more and more smoothly as you go on. Lastly which I found to be rather dumb about Hollow Knight are charms that need to be swapped out so obsolete ones such as a compass, needs to be entered inside a map and be switched manually back and forth. Bloodstained solves this issue by introducing a shortcut button where you can make a preset builds of whatever you desire, whether it be one for combat, a luck based shard system or something else entirely.

Most importantly of all I want to mention that what makes a Metroidvania game great isn't the music, artstyle or vibes. Rather, the most important thing what makes a Metroidvania great is if it encourages you to complete as much as possible, and for me. Bloodstained made that a possibility because I made sure to collect every shard, map out the whole map and fight every enemy and boss in the game.

Pick up this game whether it be on sale or not, it can go as low as 3 euros and for that, I think it's a steal. I hope the next Bloodstained game will be great as well as it seems to be heavily influenced by another Igarashi game, Portrait of Ruin which introduced the tag/partner system.

Score: 10/10

Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night is a game I really enjoyed. The sheer amount of play styles there are gives the game quite a bit of replayability. You can focus on building up your melee weapons, your different types of defensive/offensive shards (which are abilities), your armor, and your consumables. The game also never feels unfair. If you die over and over to a single boss like I did, try changing up your tactics, weapons, shards, and making sure you have enough consumables. Taking a break also helps lol. At my current playtime, 51 hours, I was able to earn every achievement, but I was really pushing for it, so if you slow your game down, you can definitely push your playtime a lot higher.

Bugs
I did encounter a bug that caused my game to crash every half hour or so. It REALLY started to get on my nerves, especially because this game has location based manual saves. I searched online and found a fix where you select a save slot different to the one you've been using, and turning off v-sync and disabling frame smoothing under settings. After all this, about 25 hours since, I haven't had a single crash.

All in all I really liked this game, especially being new to the metroidvania scene, so I would highly recommend.

My expectations for Bloodstained were very low. From its Kickstarter campaign, which heavily relied on the cult of personality surrounding Koji Igarashi, to the early graphics being a massive step down from the concept art, to its prolonged development cycle, I was expecting Bloodstained to be a mediocre game that failed to live up to its predecessors, joining the ranks of Yooka Laylee and Mighty No. 9.

Instead, Bloodstained ended up being one of the best metroidvanias I've played in years, and an easy contender for my GOTY. The combat is snappy and fluid, the music is some of Michiru Yamane's best, there are hundreds of weapons and equippables and shiny baubles to experiment with, and even though I've finished the game, I'll start on New Game+ the moment I'm finished with this review.

Ignore my playtime on Steam - I got it originally on Switch, waited MONTHS for them to fix the input lag, finished it a couple of times and then let it sit.  When I saw the wait time on the Zangetsu/Randomizer patch, and saw the Steam copy on sale I thought "screw it, let's see how much better it looks at 4K and 60FPS" and oh my... playing handheld is great and all, but it is BUTT UGLY on Switch.

I think it's pretty faithful to the core of a metroidvania and a great introduction to the genre, given that it was developed by good ole Iga-dono (who developed Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, which is where the -vania part of the portmanteau comes from).  Honestly, I'm having a hard time finding a game which is so in depth and detailed with game mechanics.  It's got everything a metroidvania should have, and more.

I love the RPG stat side of things, the upgrades and backtracking, stacking Luck to make grinding for materials and money easier. I have passed many hours on Switch just doing runs back and forth through the castle to build up my cash stocks.

I wish I could like the art more.  I admit, I'm one of those nostalgia geeks that prefers the full 2D pixel art and the 2.5D style of this isn't my favourite though I will concede that it looks so much better on PC than Switch.  The graphics on Switch are muddy and jagged at the same time, the colour pallatte muted, and just generally... uglier.  It IS a pretty game on PC, just not quite my cup o' tea.

The replayability of the game has been immensely broadened with the latest content update.  Not only can you play on harder difficulties after completing it once (as well as giving you the option to play the Boss Rush mode), you can now play the entire game as Zangetsu, or randomize the contents of loot to quite a customizable degree.  I love the idea of a lucky dip at loot locations and getting a really OP item near the start of the game, or just something new and different to what I have memorized down at this point.

I bought this on sale because I couldn't justify buying 2 full-priced copies to my fiancee (she still hates me for buying the PC copy anyways), and it's well worth the money simply on playtime alone. I love metroidvanias, and I have yet to find a new alternative that has as many features as Bloodstained.  I'm so glad we got to see a modern-day Iga-vania!

#F***Konami

P.S. If you know of any good hidden gem metroidvanias, leave a comment on the review for me!

For all its quirks and flaws, Bloodstained is Castlevania in all things but name.

I was initially rebuffed on my first playthrough; I didn't quite understand what this beast was.  I was playing as though this were a newer iteration of Symphony of the Night (SotN).  Technically, Bloodstained is a modern iteration of Aria of Sorrow (or Dawn of Sorrow).

What is the main difference between these two games, you ask?  About 20 hours of grinding.  Bloodstained even takes it a step further:  It's not enough to max out the number of monster souls (shards, whatever), you must also gather materials to improve those shards.  The long-term power gain is absolutely worth it though.

Musically, I find the game exceptional and impressive.  Visually, it's a bit of a hodgepodge.  Full 3D modeled backgrounds for a game played entirely in 2D?  Sure.  They do some interesting things with it, but it can be hard to track where the ground is supposed to be.  It helps to lean as hard as possible into the RPG mechanics to take the brunt out of inconveniences like this.

Speaking of:  The enemies are a motley collection.  I've no real complaints or criticisms, though it is still very odd and surreal to have to fight so many kickstarter backer pets.

My least favorite mechanic concerns enemies:  Contact damage is absurdly high.  The full 3D rendering does you no favors in projecting accurate hitboxes for a solid third of the enemies and most bosses.  Consider this another reason to focus on stat bolstering for survival.

Despite this, I had a pretty good time.

For the Castlevania nuts out there, this is more-or-less your "second coming." Now, I'm not going to pretend this is anything transcendent; if you weren't already sold on this being another exploration-based platformer from the guy that directed Symphony of the Night and all (but one) of the GBA/DS sequels, then perhaps this'll take a bit more explaining - after all, in the decade-plus since the last one of those came out, there's been a veritable FLOOD of Metroidvanias on Steam alone, leaving this particular one to fight against some pretty strong competition, the likes of Hollow Knight, Iconoclasts, Owlboy, and others I'm sure.

In Ritual of the Night, you are (as ever) exploring a large castle-like world. Certain paths are locked to you until you've found certain abilities to get around them, and all the while, you'll be earning experience levels and gold, finding and buying new equipment, and collecting ingredients to make some of your own. In addition to the large arsenal of equippable weapons (nearly all of which have extra fighting-game-like special attacks to find and master), you're collecting Shards that serve as a whole second page of equipment. These are all dropped by monsters on rare occasions, and if you've played Aria of Sorrow or Dawn of Sorrow, you'll know immediately how most of it works.

Overall, Ritual of the Night really isn't out to revolutionize the already-well-established Metroidvania conventions. Given how long it had been since IGA produced one himself, this game instead serves as something of a return to form, carrying the most interesting mechanics and coolest setpieces from IGA's previous fare, into feeding us older-school fans, especially ones frustrated with what Konami had been (and still is) doing with Castlevania as a series. It's more of the same, in that sense - and even despite some occasional engine jank, and some 3D cutscenes that are maybe a bit half-baked, I'd say this game's existence was long overdue. We've been starved for a real proper SOTN-like since 2008. And with ROTN, our appetites are well-catered for.

Guys, it's really good. You don't have to worry about having another Mighty Number 9 or Yooka Laylee on your hands. Igarashi and his team made a great game that is clearly a love letter to Symphony of the Night. Is it as good as SotN? No, that's impossible if only for the reason that SotN was the first time we had seen this formula. Castlevania stayed pretty true to that style of game throughout most of the handheld titles. Bloodstained has a lot in common with Aria of Sorrow and Dawn of Sorrow, given one of the central mechanics.

Enemies you kill have a chance to grant you a shard (among other loot) that behave nearly exactly like the souls you steal from enemies in the Sorrow games. Instead of having 3 categories of ability as in Sorrow, you have a few more options here. There's the standard special attack triggered with a button press, a directional attack that you can control with the analog stick, a passive slot, a manipulator slot (which seems to mostly be a catch all for things that don't really fit anywhere else), and a familiar slot. You will use all of them at the same time, and this gives you a bit of freedom when picking which elemental types you want to focus on or otherwise adjust your loadout to your playstyle.

Each shard can be upgraded in both rank and grade, with grade being an overall power boost to most abilities, and rank having various effects depending on the ability. It might increase the range of an attack or make the area of effect wider. If you fully upgrade the rank on passive shards, they become skill shards which are always equipped, freeing up your passive slot for something else. Or you can double stack the ability in both skill and passive slot for extra effect.

There's a crafting and cooking system, with food you make giving you stat bonuses that are always in effect the first time you eat each meal. These can really add up late game, and you'll probably be trying to find freakin' soy sauce forever to craft some of the food in your list. There's also a quest system, but it isn't anything special. The quests have three main varieties; bring this NPC a certain food item, kill a certain number of a certain type of demon, or bring an NPC a certain item. 

There are a lot of weapon types, similar to SotN, and each type behaves differently. Knives are fast but have almost no range, whips have a slight wind up but cover a pretty decent area in front of you, and guns do gun things by shooting bullets, just to give a few examples. The weapons and armor also have various elements and damage types that they can deal or protect against, so stacking the right resist for a boss can really make a big difference.

The map is pretty large, and has a bunch of nods to SotN. If you are familiar with SotN, you'll come across many places that you remember such as the huge underground waterfall. You'll notice familiar enemy types as well, even if they look different. Flying medusa heads are here, but they aren't actually medusa heads. Still, when you see them you'll know you're gonna get petrified. The game is harder than SotN, but it isn't a hard game. It just doesn't have any super broken gear that is easily obtained and lets you faceroll the whole game without trying, like the Crissaegrim. (edit: Okay, I found this game's Crissaegrim so I take that back.)

It sure doesn't look as amazing as SotN, however. Symphony has some of the best pixel art of all time, with some gigantic ass enemies that are only in one or two spots and would be bosses in any other game. It isn't ugly by any means, but I don't think it holds a candle to the game it is mimicking. 

If you like this style of Castlevania, get it. If you've played SotN, you know what to expect with the story and playing past the "final" boss, but even then it's still a ton of fun.

Bloodstained ROTN is a really good Metroidvania game and a satisfying Castlevania game. For reference. the only Castlevania games I played as a kid are Harmony of Dissonance, Aria of Sorrow, and Dawn of Sorrow. Out of the three, Aria of Sorrow is my most favorite and I really feel Aria of Sorrow in Bloodstained. From the music, to gameplay, its really good. 

Some mechanics of the game (crafting etc.) requires grinding enemies and looting chests. And those mechanics really help in defeating strong enemies. I don't mind them as I didn't grind as much, but some people might find it to be annoying.

I want so much to love this game, but I just can't recommend it for a host of reasons. First, though, the good stuff.

-This is very obviously a love letter to Symphony of the Night. In that sense, it succeeds. 
-Like its inspiration, it boasts an absurd number of weapons with different abilities. Where combat in metroidvanias can often get stale, this is quite nice.
-Enemies are generally varied and require different approaches to fight.
-While level design is hit-or-miss, the ones that work, like the cathedral area, work extremely well.
-Most importantly, the core gameplay is generally fun, with some notable exceptions (see below).

So, with all of that, why wouldn't I recommend this game? 

-The single worst thing in this game is the way you need to farm. Now, sure, you can ignore the sidequests and most of the crafting and this won't be a problem, but if you *do* engage with these systems the bottlenecks are just stupid. Often there are drops that are you  a) need six or more of, b) only drop off two mobs (not two mob types, but *two mobs in the game*), and c) have a sub 10% drop rate. The result is that if you choose to do the side quests or engage with the crafting you're forced to spam kill the same mob repeatedly, for far too long

The same problem exists with the self-replenishing chests, except that the drop locations for chest-only items doesn't update your archive, meaning you'd better be paying close attention to where you get rare chest drops.

In the end, you don't need any of this gear, either, so it's just for completionism. There's no content that demands this harder-to-get gear, which makes its inclusion mystifying. Sure, this is similar to SOTN, which had rare drops that were completely unnecessary to the endgame, but that was a flaw in the original we didn't need to see replicated twenty years later.
-Some of the fights are just poorly designed. This is subjective, obviously, but it seems pretty clear which bosses and which regular mobs got the most time and testing--some are excellent and engaging, and others just have poor signalling and no clear way to avoid taking damage even when you see it coming. This is compounded by the next problem.
-Another holdover from  SOTN is the straightforward leveling system. Just as in that game, it's a terrible kludge. Learning the fights is unnecessary because you can just level and bludgeon through them, and at the same time it allows for some lazy fight design because this is always an option for the players. 
-The levels that are badly designed are just awful. Because of the prevalence of enemies that ignore geometry, the levels that work best are the ones with significant amounts of open space. The Inferno Caves, in particular, feel like they were designed to be annoying. The cookie-cutter elemental enemies and bugs flying through the landscape make you feel like you're fighting the terrain more than the enemies. It's lazy design, not interesting, and less fun.
-That this game has performance issues is another unforgivable callback to SOTN. As others have mentioned, this game has periodic slowdowns despite looking like a ten-year old game. I'm fine with the visual style--it's half of why i bought it--but there's no reason for this to have issues running on a new, high-end machine.
-While I appreciate the homage to SOTN, it's *exactly* like SOTN, down to what passes for story. SOTN was an amazing game for its time, but many other games in the genre have made significant improvements in the intervening twenty years, and it feels like the developers have been locked in a time capsule. 
-Last, price. For a game that's basically just aped SOTN without adding anything new of note it's very expensive. I know they're adding new content, which is welcome, but it doesn't even have SOTN's ability to play Richter.

My other objections are extremely subjective:
-The general castle design just wasn't remotely interesting and made zero attempt making physical sense. No, SOTN didn't do this either, but again, it's been twenty years. Putting the Japanese garden in the sky over the cathedral towers was just weird. On top of that, some of the areas were just bland or nonsensical. Why are the Halls of Termination called that? They're...gilded. It's weird. This, plus the multiple labs that use the same tileset, the super-generic "fire level", were just bad. There's an initial logic--the castle entry over a watery moat that descends into an underwater area--gets more or less discarded in the later game.
-The side quests / minor characters are unforgivably cut/paste fetch quests when you consider this is a $40 game.  They couldn't even be bothered to write new or changing flavor text for most of it.
-The story is just...bad. I could write an entire essay on this so I'm just going to stop myself. It's a SOTN reskin.
-Last, the music. It's not terrible, but it's entirely forgettable. It's like someone set out to create Castlevania-esque music but didn't give a lot of thought to the setting of each area or to creating any real mood. 

Overall, if anyone makes it this far, this is a game that had promise but just didn't deliver in too many ways. You can spend half the money and get a game that's superior in every way in Hollow Knight.

A worthy successor to Symphony of the Night this most certainly is not. The game is... fine, I guess. The whole thing just feels cheap and amateurish.

1. The visuals are not good; there's no cohesive art direction here. Many textures are substandard, rooms are filled with tiled assets and clashing colors, and the high gloss visual style is strange and ill-suited to the intended aesthetic. Animations feel unfinished. Enemy designs are all over the place. The game's visual presentation is like a giant melting pot in which nothing has melted.

2. The controls are adequate, but that's the best that can be said of them. Enemy hit boxes are hard to identify, so you'll never get to perfectly gauge that "just right" distance like you could in Symphony. The majority of the weapons have a windup animation, limiting the ones that I'd consider usable or fun to the ones that respond immediately. Jumping is quick and snappy, but colliding with the environment feels... off. Other games in the genre do this right, so what gives? This was the main area that the game needed to excel in, and it didn't. At all.

3. Too much lame filler content. There's a town area where you can make food, take on quests, upgrade weapons, etc. All of it just feels like a tedious time sink. It's not fun. It's not very rewarding. The dialogue is dreadful, so it's not like talking to the townspeople is worthwhile outside of their mechanical purpose. This entire area could have (should have) been scrapped. All of it would have been just as easy to do from a single menu option. The farmer? Why is this guy even in the game? It's pure, exceptionally weak filler content to pad the game out.

4. The music is not good. A couple of memorable songs, but just as many obnoxious ones with the rest being totally forgettable. The library (whatever area that vampire salesman is in) music is just awful. I couldn't believe what I was hearing - I actually laughed out loud and recorded it on my phone to send to a friend. There are many metroidvania games on Steam, but as someone who fell in love with this little side scrolling sub-genre with Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, its spiritual successor, Bloodstained, is my favorite. Having played basically all of Koji Igarashi’s Castlevania titles, I can confidently say there is not a god damned thing about Bloodstained’s gameplay, story or aesthetics that is original in any meaningful way; it’s a greatest hits compilation by your favorite band except the lead singer has been replaced after dying in the bathroom of a heroin overdose. Fortunately, the saga of the Belmonts versus Dracula is not what made Castlevania a classic franchise so Bloodstained does not suffer in their absence.

Bloodstained’s plot centers around a shardbinder (a human imbuned with magical powers via demonic crystals) a human named Miriam, who is trying to track down and stop another, more dastardly shard binder named Gebel. There are more elements at play, (exorcists, a demon hunting samurai, a surviving member of the alchemy guild that created the shardbinders, etc.) but it’s all just a non-vampire related reason to storm a castle and hack a bunch of creatures to death. Fans of Igarashi’s previous works will find very familiar plot elements in play and there is enough narrative for people interested to chew on while those of us who are less invested in the anime-esque proceedings are not forced to wade through tons of dialog and tedious lore. 

Miriam is a master of a number of weapons: swords, axes, spears, firearms, daggers and whips (of course) and she can collect shards from fallen enemies which can be used to cast spells. This system will be familiar to those who played Aria of Sorrow and Dawn of Sorrow, compelling players to linger around rooms with new enemies and farm them for new abilities. The more shards that are collected for a specific spell, the more powerful it grows and shards can be upgraded in the game’s hub area. Weapons have vastly different attack speeds, angles of attack, and effective ranges giving players numerous options to tailor their loadout to their playstyle and keeping things from being as simple as equipping the item with the best stats. Different weapons also have special attacks and Miriam can also backdash and slide to spice up the gameplay further. All of this is very familiar to Castlevania fans and all of the inputs feel right and there are enough elements to tweak and adjust when you are having difficulty slaying a boss or making it through a new area. 

Apart from the shard collecting, those prone to being addicted to collecting and crafting in game items will be pleased to learn of what might be Bloodstained’s most original element, crafting food for permanent stat boosts. Essentially Miriam can find several recipe books and various ingredients are dropped by enemies or found in chests, these can be taken back to the hub area and crafted into delicious dishes. Every time Miriam eats a new dish she gets a permanent stat boost. It’s an enjoyable diversion to see what ingredients are needed and try to remember what enemies dropped those ingredients as well as a great way for players who are struggling to gain an edge.

Where Bloodstained could become a little divisive is in its difficulty. Metroidvania games often tend to be somewhat difficult, but Bloodstained errs toward being more approachable and forgiving. The Castlevania titles released under Igarashi’s watch ran the gamut of difficulty levels, which became a source of frustration for some fans, particularly those who grew up on the hard-as-nails level based games that came before Symphony of the Night. Personally, I don’t see a problem with the game’s difficulty since players are penalized for their lack of skill by being forced to dedicate more time to grinding cash and raw materials for crafting so that they can gain an edge. 

Bloodstained is to Castlevania what Singer is to Porsche. It peels away the various successful elements of previous iterations and sews them all together for a definitive sample platter of a decade’s worth of games. Everyone will have their nit-picks about which element from which game is better, but I think a vast majority would walk away from Bloodstained feeling that it’s a worthy successor to a franchise that is basically dead.

I'm enjoying the game. So why is the review negative, you ask? Well, because I must warn players of a few things, and given that this game has Overwhelmingly Positive reviews, if I made the review positive, my warnings would just get lost among the other flood of positive reviews. A negative one catches the eye a lot more in this case, as it probably did yours. Anyway, moving on.

The thing I must warn players about is that this game is, on purpose, designed with OUTDATED mechanics. Igarashi wanted to give Castlevania players a blast from the past, and apparently that includes not keeping up with 20 years in game design advancements. If you're used to metroidvanias or roguelikes with fluid movement and fast-paced combat (such as Rogue Legacy, Dead Cells, Hades etc.), or in other words, modern game design, you will right away be baffled by:

[list]
[*]  how slow, clunky and heavy Miriam feels overall. If you're used to Hollow Knight or similar, you will DESPISE how movement and combat feels in this game. Especially since you don't really have dashing abilities (just a kind of half-dash/step, and only backwards) and don't get double jump until some 5-10 hours into the game. Maybe you get a forward dash later, I don't know.

[*] This one drives me NUTS: for many attacks, Miriam will move slightly forward after each attack, meaning that if you're right in front of an enemy, attacking can cause you to briefly and lightly touch the enemy, doing FULL DAMAGE to you. AAAAAARRRRGGGGGHHHH. This also happens when, for instance, you kick an enemy and do damage to it, but when Miriam retracts or lowers her leg after the attack, her leg touches any part of the enemy. Full damage again. Very frustrating. While this can also happen in other metroidvanias such as Blasphemous, at least they had the good sense of making contact damage only a small fraction of the damage you get when the enemy hits you with an actual attack.

[*] The absence of any real combos; pressing attack multiple times with any weapon will simply attack exactly the same way multiple times, without any variation even to the animations used or the direction the weapon is swung from.

[*] Most weapons have a long-ass cooldown animation after attacking which stop you from attacking again. The only "combo" mechanics available are what are called "animation cancels": if you attack right before landing, then attack right away after landing, you'll bypass the cooldown and be able to attack twice in a row. If you then do a step dodge backwards, you can attack quickly a third time. To make it clear: this is not a bug, this is considered a [b]feature[/b] that players are expected to take advantage of. Since I can't be bothered to time this process just right, I just use the fastest weapons I can find instead, since they don't have a long cooldown animation anyway.
[/list]
