It's with a great amount of hesitation and trepidation that I recommend Bloodstained. My play time is notably marked by a good chunk of idle/afk time stepping away to help with a baby-in-need, but I did play the game all the way through, got 100% on achievements, and all that fun jazz. My save file clocked in around 25 years for 100% achievements. I suppose I enjoy completing these types of games, regardless of quality, because I've been playing Metroidvanias since I was wee tot back in Super Metroid and Castlevania: Circle of the Moon. As with Hollow Knight, I felt my expectations for the title were shaped a lot based on hype: Bloodstained was supposed to be *the* successor to Symphony of the Night. It sat on my desktop for something like 4 years as I scraped through various other titles and genres, and the "big reveal" on finally completing the game has left me pretty jaded.

On one hand, the game has some truly great moments and fights that just feel beautifully composed and memorable. On the other, it has some moments that made me incredibly frustrated because I simply couldn't figure out the precise interaction required because of poorly-designed game UI decisions. For example, in most Metroidvania games you have "combat" skills and "utility" skills that are clearly delineated. In Bloodstained, you may kill a boss and get a red "combat" skill that's in with all the others which have a 100% strict combat use...but there will be one singular interaction in the game where it's used for a non-combat purpose. Or another example, there are objects that can be pushed or moved with a utility skill you get early in the game. Every object that is to be interacted with by this skill is highlighted...except one specific object that appears in two locations in the game which is not. Naturally, I thought bypassing this object would thus require a different skill obtained by defeating some other boss until I had the map completely explored and literally nowhere else to go. Looking it up in a guide was an immediate "oh okay, duh" moment, but the game does not organically assist you in reaching these decisions due to conflicting presentations of interactions.

With that in mind, I did still enjoy Bloodstained. How excited I will be in the future to return to this title I am not sure, but I do generally enjoy playing a Metroidvania title through 100% completion and I did feel it fun to tick all the collector boxes and complete a save file. My fun, however, did not really stem from a deep enjoyment of the game itself -- there are a ton of weapons which you'll never really use, even more skills you'll never interact with, and a crafting system with some odd "grind this 1% time a ridiculous number of times" that's made feasible by stacking luck to crazy levels. All-in-all, the controls are a bit clunky and unresponsive, as you tend to get locked into animations for a large count of frames. Things like backstep were just never used because it usually makes no difference as to whether you'll be hit or not. Ignoring all this, you can still dodge (relatively well) with jumps and animation cancelling on certain combinations, so the game does not feel horribly difficult to navigate. The game is good, but it's hardly a brilliant Castlevania successor.

Play at your own peril, I suppose, provided you have proper expectations. The game promised itself as far more than it actually delivers, and the big price tag is not really justified for the quality of product received. Get it on sale like I did and it's probably worth it for people who enjoy the genre. Disappointing but certainly playable once through.

I can probably count the number of game developers who came back from a decade-long hiatus on the fingers of one hand, let alone as much success and popularity as Koji Igarashi had garnered at the height of his career as a game developer. In an industry that's full of washed-up has-beens and frauds masquerading as creators - all of whom seem a tad too busy riding the coattails of their past glory to produce anything even mildly entertaining or creative, It's refreshing to see one creator that not only didn't succumb to the ravages of time, but rather silently honed his spirit and resolve, ultimately producing one of the finest games the genre has to offer.

Perhaps somewhat contrary to what has been said before, Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night doesn't reinvent the wheel by any means. Nearly every mechanic in this game has been done before in previous titles that Koji had worked on, such as gravity flipping or soul collecting, except here it has been polished to a mirror shine. In essence, the same things that apply to previous games in the genre apply here too: The levels are large and sprawling and require a great deal of backtracking if one wishes to find all the extra bosses, loot, easter eggs, and general lore the game has to offer. The platforming is as good as it has ever been and the combat and boss encounters seem to be unique and memorable, as well as the myriad of colorful characters the game throws at you every now and then. The story isn't exactly revolutionary, but it gets the job done reasonably well. The Kickstarter promises that the developers said will come eventually are taking their sweet time to get here, but the ones that are already delivered seem to be well implemented and add a ton of replay value to what is already an impressively long game on its own.

In summary, there is no shortage of content here for pretty much any person of any skill level who happens to like action-platformers. Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night is what happens when egos aren't running out of control and there is enough freedom and willingness to listen to what fans of the genre had been wanting all along - an extremely rare event in today's industry even among crowdfunded projects.

This is not a bad game. It's just not a great game that deserves overwhelmingly positive. It has a lot of issues that really bogged the game down for me.

The first biggest issue is the game progression. There were four instances where I got stuck and was not sure where to go next. One of those times, I actually stumbled upon what to do completely by accident, and when I discovered it, I was immediately pissed off and knew I would use a guide next time I got stuck, which didn't take too long. Let me tell you exactly where you will probably get stuck and why.

The first time is after you beat a boss and get the material to make a photograph. You have the photograph, now what? The only area you haven't explored is a train station that won't open for you. You need the photograph to make an ID to get in. So you go around talking to the NPCs and they offer you no help. Actually you are supposed to talk to an NPC, but it's the only one that's not marked on your map. All he does is loan you books that give you power. You're supposed to randomly go back to him and talk to him and he'll just give you the ID you need. Cool...

The next time is after you get the ability to drain blood. There's an obvious blood fountain that you can't forget in the first area. You immediately go there and drain the fountain. You explore a little, but you quickly get stopped by some water. You can't swim. "I need to find the swimming ability." Guess where the swimming ability is. You have to kill a regular enemy that's in the water and it has a (high) chance of dropping the swimming ability. Every other time, abilities are given by bosses. I saw the regular enemy, but I didn't want to kill it because it was in the water, and obviously it would be easier to kill it if I were swimming too.

The third time you'll get stuck is after you can invert the world. There's an obvious path to go on again, but there are spikes in the way. How do you get through the spikes? There are two single squares on the map that you could not fill in in a giant tower that was used for a boss fight. Go there and one side has a treasure chest. If you explore the other side and see nothing, maybe you'll get discouraged from checking the other side. I didn't check either side because it's just a boss room. I'll save exploring for right before the boss. Stupid me. This is the only time a random treasure chest is needed to progress.

The final time is after you get the Zangetsuto. You know you need it to kill a boss, but what boss? The only boss left is one that if you kill, you get a game over. You're supposed to fight him and get him very close to death and then stop looking at the boss to notice the moon changes colors and then slash the moon. I figured the boss was the way to go, but I was too distracted by the boss to notice the moon changing colors before I killed him.

Those four events really soured the game for me. That is simply unintuitive design. Aside from that, the second biggest issue I have with the game is the lack of polish. The way the character model interacts with walls looks straight out of a PS2 game with crazy amounts of clipping. It's very jarring and always puts me off. Then there's a lot of hitbox issues. One time I got stuck in the floor and couldn't escape. My character was stuck bouncing up and down and I could only move left or right I eventually wriggled myself free, but it looked so terrible. Enemies (especially bosses) seem to give me touch damage even when I'm clearly not touching them. Cutscenes were broken for me. For whatever reason, cutscenes had no sound for me except sometimes there was some light background music. There were no voices or sound effects. And if you have an ultrawide screen like me, the only way you can play is borderless fullscreen with pillarboxes that has graphical issues. Fullscreen (the default option) stretches the image. Borderless fixes the stretching, but I could see a side of a red and blue rectangle in the pillarboxes for whatever reason. And in the menus and quest screens, you can see the subscreens on the sides where you're not supposed to see. The mods to fix ultrawide didn't work for me. Pitiful for a modern game to not have more support for widescreen. Even proper pillarboxing is fine for me.

There are some other minor issues as well, such as I really didn't like any of the boss fights. They all feel like sponges to me and take an insane number of hits to kill. They all have such a long delay in between attacks that you're just constantly spamming attack. And then when they do attack, it feels like there's no wind-up animation for you to properly react to them. That's fine for some games and means you should play defensively, but since the enemies are such sponges, you really don't want to go defensive and deal with a 10 minute drag of a fight. I ended up not caring about being hit and just spamming attacks as fast as I could and just chugging potions and such to get the fight over with.

Speaking of potions, this game has crafting in it, and it's terrible. You need crafting for better weapons, armor, and food (potions). Finding ingredients is a real pain. For over half the game, I barely touched food because I could not find ingredients. Throughout my adventures killing all enemies I came across, I did not get many key ingredients needed to craft the foods. There is a food questline, and I for the longest time could not figure out why I was not progressing in it. Then I decided to finally look up what ingredients I was missing and go farm it. So I farmed for the food I couldn't make and got to the next food. Oh. I don't have those ingredients either... Quests should be able to be progressed naturally and not need such immense farming. Why can't the weapons and armor be in chests or monster drops like other Castlevanias? Some monsters do drop some, but 90% is from crafting.

Overall, I was sorely disappointed with Ritual of the Night. I loved every single minute of Curse of the Moon 1 and 2, and I like the exploration Castlevanias more than the linear oldschool ones, so I was eagerly awaiting Ritual of the Night. Just play those games instead and play SotN or the GBA/DS Castlevanias if you want your fix. This game is not bad by any means, but it could have been so much better.
